mainTopic: Trusting surveyors of the תחום שבת, and making an ערוב for a city that changed between private and public
overview: The גמרא first finishes the משנה about measuring the תחום שבת. It explains that a surveyor is trusted even when he extends the limit, and that when two surveyors disagree, we follow the one who extended. אביי limits this: the extra amount may not exceed the difference made by measuring along the diagonal. רבינא resolves a contradiction about whether חכמים were lenient or strict here. The system of תחומין was made as a stringency, but because it is only דרבנן, its measuring details may be lenient. A new משנה then turns to עירובי חצירות. A private city that became public may have one ערוב for all of it, but a public city that became private must leave a section outside the ערוב, and רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון argue about that section's size. The גמרא asks for an example of a private city that became public. רב יהודה names the ריש גלותא's village, while רב נחמן challenges that example and names the village of נתזואי instead. A ברייתא explains how to include a real רשות הרבים in such a city and forbids an ערוב for half the city. It then begins the case of a city that was always public, whose ruling comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Why only where he extended?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the משנה's phrase 'in a place where he extended, we listen to him.' Does that mean we would not listen to him where he reduced?
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Where he extended the limit, yes we listen; where he reduced it, no?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by questioning a phrase in the משנה. The words seem to say we trust the surveyor only when he extends the תחום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Trusting someone who extends the limit is the bigger leniency. Trusting someone who shrinks it is only a stringency, and everyone accepts a stringency. So the wording 'where he extended' looks strange, as if a shortened measurement would be rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA:
To a place where he extended — yes (we listen),
but to a place where he reduced — no?
phrases.notes: He's asking in surprise: of course we should accept it when he made the area smaller!

steps.triggerLanguage: לִמְקוֹם שֶׁרִיבָּה אִין, לִמְקוֹם שֶׁמִּיעֵט לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the end of the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's wording 'במקום שריבה שומעין לו'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wording implies we reject a reduction. That makes no sense, because a stringent measurement should certainly be accepted.

steps.title: Read it as 'even where he extended'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה means we listen to him even where he extended. Where he reduced, we certainly listen.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say: even to a place where he extended.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the question by rereading the משנה. Add the word 'even': we trust the surveyor even when he extends the limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה is not excluding reductions. It is teaching the bigger חידוש: even an extension is trusted, and we do not worry that he made a mistake. A reduction is obviously accepted.

phrases.english: Say (read it as):
even to a place where he extended.

steps.terutzMaskana: Even extended measurements are accepted, and reduced ones certainly are

steps.title: Isn't the next clause a repeat?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next clause, 'he extended for one and reduced for another.' It asks why this is needed, since it seems to say the same thing again.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He extended for one and reduced for another…' Why do I need this too? It is the same as that!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה. It complains that this line seems to repeat what was just taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we know the surveyor is trusted even when he extends, the clause about extending for one and reducing for another seems to add nothing. The גמרא assumes the משנה does not waste words, so this clause must teach something new.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need this as well?
This is the same as that
Etc. (the quote continues in the משנה)

steps.confusionAlert: The first line is only a quotation from the משנה (a 'heading'). The actual challenge begins with הָא תּוּ לְמָה לִי.

phrases.english: 'He extended for one and reduced for another, etc.'
phrases.notes: This line is quoted from the משנה.

phrases.english: Why do I need this as well?
It is the same as that!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא תּוּ לְמָה לִי? הַיְינוּ הָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next clause of the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It appears redundant with the previous clause about trusting an extension.

steps.title: It means two different surveyors
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the clause is about two surveyors. One extended and one reduced, and we follow the one who extended.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: one surveyor extended and one reduced — we listen to the one who extended.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the clause is not a repeat. It describes a new case of two surveyors who disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'לאחד … לאחד' are reread as 'אחד … אחד,' meaning one person and another person. The new teaching is that when two measurements conflict, we follow the more lenient, larger one.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it is saying

steps.whatToRemember: There are two rules here. One surveyor is trusted even when he extends the תחום. When two surveyors disagree, we follow the one who extended.

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:
one (surveyor) extended and one reduced —
we listen to the one who extended.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (one surveyor → two surveyors)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The clause repeats the single-surveyor case
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause teaches that we follow the extending surveyor when two surveyors conflict

steps.title: אביי limits how much extra we accept
steps.stepSummary: אביי rules that we follow the extending surveyor only if his extra amount is no more than the difference made by measuring along the diagonal.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: As long as he does not extend more than the measure of the city along the diagonal.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי adds a limit to the rule that we follow the surveyor who extended.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The city and its תחום are treated as a square, so the corner reaches farther along the diagonal than straight out from the side. We can explain the disagreement as one surveyor measuring diagonally and the other measuring straight. If the gap is bigger than that diagonal difference, the explanation fails. Then we cannot rely on the larger measurement.

keyTerms.meaning: Provided that / only as long as
The measurement of the city (its תחום)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the leniency has a logical basis: we can explain why the measurements differ. The leniency stops where that explanation stops.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
provided that he does not extend
more than the measure of the city along the diagonal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Qualifies the rule established in step 4
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We follow the extending surveyor only if the gap does not exceed the diagonal-versus-straight difference

steps.title: Lenient or strict? A ברייתא contradicts the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's reason, that חכמים were lenient here. It then challenges it with a ברייתא that says חכמים were strict.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'For חכמים did not say the matter to be strict, but to be lenient.' But wasn't it taught: חכמים did not say the matter to be lenient, but to be strict?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the reason given in the משנה. It sets up a contradiction from a ברייתא that says the exact opposite, and the answer will come in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the rules of תחומין were given for leniency, which is why we trust extensions. A ברייתא says these rules were given for stringency. Both cannot be true as stated, so the גמרא must reconcile them.
steps.confusionAlert: The first sentence is the משנה. The second sentence, after וְהָתַנְיָא, is the opposing ברייתא. The wording is almost identical except that להקל and להחמיר switch places.

phrases.english: 'For the Sages did not state the matter'
phrases.notes: This line is quoted from the משנה.

phrases.english: to be strict, but rather to be lenient.'
But wasn't it taught (in a ברייתא):
The Sages did not state the matter
to be lenient, but rather to be strict?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: לֹא אָמְרוּ חֲכָמִים אֶת הַדָּבָר לְהָקֵל אֶלָּא לְהַחֲמִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the משנה's stated reason and challenges it
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's principle 'לא אמרו חכמים את הדבר להחמיר אלא להקל'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא states the opposite principle: the rules were said for stringency, not leniency.

steps.title: רבינא explains how חכמים can be both strict and lenient
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that תחומין as a whole were created to be stricter than Torah law. Since they are only rabbinic, חכמים allowed leniency in how they are measured.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: חכמים did not set up תחומין to be more lenient than Torah law. They set them up to be stricter than Torah law. And since תחומין are only דרבנן, we can be lenient in measuring them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the contradiction from Step 6. The משנה said חכמים were lenient, and the ברייתא said they were strict.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two sources are talking about two different things. The ברייתא's 'strict' describes why the whole system of תחומין exists: to add a limit beyond Torah law. The משנה's 'lenient' describes the details of measuring. Since the whole system is only דרבנן, being lenient in its details is fine.

keyTerms.meaning: Shabbat boundaries (how far one may walk outside a city)

steps.whatToRemember: The system of תחומין was created as a stringency. Because it is only דרבנן, חכמים may be lenient in how it is measured, such as listening to the surveyor who extended.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a common principle: in a rabbinic law, we can be lenient on the details, even though the law itself was made as a stringency.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
Not to be lenient compared to Torah law,
phrases.notes: This describes why the system of תחומין was set up.

phrases.english: but rather to be strict beyond Torah law,
and Shabbat limits are rabbinic.
phrases.notes: This is why leniency in measuring is allowed.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא לְהָקֵל עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא לְהַחְמִיר עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the two sources: one talks about why the system exists, the other about how it is carried out.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and ברייתא seem to directly contradict each other about whether חכמים were lenient or strict.
steps.terutzMaskana: The system was created as a stringency. Its measuring details, being דרבנן, allow leniency.

steps.title: A private city that became public may have one ערוב
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that if a private city becomes a public city, one ערוב may be made for the entire city.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A city that belonged to an individual and became a public city: one may make an ערוב for all of it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It goes back to the laws of joining courtyards (עירובי חצירות) and opens with a city that changed from private to public.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The city started out private, so it never had the status of a public city where carrying was clearly forbidden. Even after it grows, one ערוב can cover the whole city. This is allowed as long as there is no Torah-level רשות הרבים in it.

keyTerms.meaning: a private city (belonging to one person, with few residents)
a public city with many residents
we make an ערוב (joining of courtyards)

steps.confusionAlert: This משנה is about עירובי חצירות, which let people carry between courtyards. It is not about the תחומי שבת (walking limits) discussed just before.

phrases.english: MISHNA: A city of an individual,
which became a city of the public —
one may make an eruv for all of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ עִיר שֶׁל יָחִיד וְנַעֲשֵׂית שֶׁל רַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the measuring discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A private city that became public may be included in one ערוב for the whole city.

steps.title: A public city that became private needs an area left out
steps.stepSummary: If a public city becomes private, one ערוב may not cover all of it unless part of the city is left outside. רבי יהודה says that part must be the size of the town of חדשה (fifty residents). רבי שמעון says three courtyards with two houses each is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a public city that became private: one may not make an ערוב for all of it unless he leaves an area outside it, like the town of חדשה in יהודה, which has fifty residents. These are the words of רבי יהודה. רבי שמעון says: three courtyards of two houses each.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the opposite case, a public city that became private. It requires part of the city to be left outside the ערוב, and two תנאים argue about how big that part must be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once a city was public, people remember carrying there as forbidden. If one ערוב covered everything, they might forget that carrying in a public place needs an ערוב. Leaving one section outside, where carrying stays forbidden, keeps the memory alive. רבי יהודה requires a large area (fifty residents). רבי שמעון accepts a much smaller one (three courtyards with two houses each).

keyTerms.meaning: outside it (an area left out of the ערוב)
the town of חדשה in יהודה, used as a size standard

steps.whatToRemember: A city that went from private to public may have one ערוב for everything. A city that went from public to private must leave a section outside the ערוב. רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון argue about that section's size.

phrases.english: And a public city that became private —
one may not make an eruv for all of it

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן עָשָׂה חוּצָה לָהּ.
phrases.english: unless he leaves an area outside it,
like the town of Chadasha in Judea,
phrases.notes: This gives the size of the area that must be left out.

phrases.english: which has fifty residents,
these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Shimon says:
three courtyards of two houses each.
phrases.notes: A much smaller area is enough to leave out.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשֶׁל רַבִּים וְנַעֲשֵׂית שֶׁל יָחִיד אֵין מְעָרְבִין אֶת כּוּלָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite case to Step 8 and adds a dispute between תנאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A public city that became private cannot have one ערוב for everything unless a section is left out. רבי יהודה requires fifty residents' worth. רבי שמעון requires three courtyards of two houses each.

steps.title: What is an example of a private city that became public?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a real case of a private city that turned into a public city.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What are the circumstances of a private city that became a public city?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by asking for a concrete example of the משנה's first case. This sets up רב יהודה's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is hard to picture a city that is 'private' and then 'public.' The גמרא wants a real situation so we know exactly what the משנה means. It is not challenging the ruling, only defining the case.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the case? / how do we picture it?

phrases.english: GEMARA: What are the circumstances

phrases.aramaic: עִיר שֶׁל יָחִיד וְנַעֲשֵׂית שֶׁל רַבִּים?
phrases.english: of a private city that became a public city?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי עִיר שֶׁל יָחִיד וְנַעֲשֵׂית שֶׁל רַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a real example of the case in Step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A real-life example of a private city that became public.

steps.title: The ריש גלותא's village as the example
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה answers that the village of the ריש גלותא is an example.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: For example, the village of the ריש גלותא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question from Step 10 with a well-known real place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ריש גלותא's village was originally a small private settlement for his family and attendants. So many people kept coming there that it grew into a public city. That is exactly the משנה's first case.

keyTerms.meaning: the Exilarch, leader of the Jews in Babylonia

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
For example, the village of the Exilarch.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה כְּגוֹן דִּאיסְקַרְתָּא דְּרֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ריש גלותא's village, which began private and became public because so many people came there.

steps.title: רב נחמן questions the example of the ריש גלותא's village
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks what makes the ריש גלותא's village a special example. He rejects the likely reason, that people gather there and remind each other of the rules, because all Jews gather every שבת morning anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to him: What is the reason you chose that example? If you say it is because people are found at the governor's place and remind each other of the rule, then all of the Jewish people also gather together on שבת morning.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן challenges רב יהודה's example from the previous step. He argues that the reason that would make this village special is not really special at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Choosing the ריש גלותא's village suggests something unique about it. The likely reason is that crowds come to the governor's office and remind each other why an ערוב is allowed there, so no one will copy it in the wrong place. רב נחמן answers that every Jewish community meets in shul on שבת morning, so that reminder exists everywhere and does not make this village unique.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (the גמרא offers a possible reason in order to reject it)
The governor or official authority, whose office people visited for permits

steps.confusionAlert: רב נחמן is not arguing with the halacha of the משנה. He only disputes whether רב יהודה's example is a good or special illustration of it.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said to him:
What is the reason (for this example)?
If you say it is because people are found at the governor's place,
phrases.notes: Many people came to the governor's office to request permits.

phrases.english: and they remind one another (of the reason it is permitted)
then all of the Jewish people also
are found together on שבת morning.
phrases.notes: They gather for davening, so they could remind each other in any town.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן: מַאי טַעְמָא? אִילֵּימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the example given by רב יהודה in step 11
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's choice of the ריש גלותא's village as the example
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The reason that would make this village special, people gathering and reminding each other, applies to every Jewish town on שבת morning, so the example is not unique.

steps.title: רב נחמן's own example: the village of נתזואי
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן offers a different example of a private city that became public: the village of נתזואי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן said: An example is the village of נתזואי.
steps.whatsHappening: Having rejected רב יהודה's example, רב נחמן gives his own answer to the question from step 10.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נתזואי was a private estate owned by one person that later filled with many residents and became public. It fits the משנה's case simply, without needing any special reason such as people reminding each other.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Nachman said:
For example, the village of Natzu'i.
phrases.notes: It once belonged to one owner and later became a public town.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the example that רב נחמן rejected in step 12
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A real case of a private city that became public (step 10)

steps.title: How to make an ערוב when a public road runs through the city
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if a once-private city becomes public and a real רשות הרבים passes through it, one places a לחי or a קורה at each end of that road. One may then carry in between.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A private city that became public, with a public domain passing through it, how does one make an ערוב for it? He puts a side post here and a side post there, or a crossbeam here and a crossbeam there, and he may carry in the middle.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a harder version of the משנה's case: a real public road runs through the city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A true רשות הרבים normally blocks carrying and cannot be fixed with a simple marker. Here the ברייתא rules that a symbolic לחי or קורה at each end of the road is enough, though it does not state the reason. That stretch of road then counts like one of the city's courtyards, so one may carry there.

keyTerms.meaning: A true public domain where carrying is forbidden
A side post placed at the opening of an alley
A crossbeam placed over the opening of an alley

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how far the leniency for a once-private city goes: even a real public road inside it can be included with only symbolic markers.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: עִיר שֶׁל יָחִיד וְנַעֲשֵׂית שֶׁל רַבִּים
phrases.english: A city of an individual that became a city of the many
and a public domain passes through it,
how does one make an ערוב for it?
He makes a side post here and a side post there,
phrases.notes: One at each end of the public road.

phrases.english: or a crossbeam here and a crossbeam there,
and he may carry in the middle.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: עִיר שֶׁל יָחִיד וְנַעֲשֵׂית שֶׁל רַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the משנה's rule from step 8 to a city with a true public road inside it
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A לחי or a קורה at each end of the public road allows carrying in that stretch as part of the city's ערוב.

steps.title: No ערוב for half the city
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that one cannot make an ערוב for half the city. It must be either the whole city or each alley on its own.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one may not make an ערוב for it in halves. Rather, either all of it together, or each alley by itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and sets a limit on how the ערוב may be divided.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the city is treated as one unit, there are only two choices. One ערוב can cover the whole city, or each alley can make its own ערוב. Splitting the city into two big halves is not allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: An alley that several courtyards open into

steps.whatToRemember: For a private city that became public: a לחי or a קורה at each end of a public road through it is enough, and the ערוב covers either the whole city or each alley separately, never half.

phrases.english: And one may not make an ערוב for it in halves,
rather, either all of it,
or each alley by itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a limit on dividing the ערוב
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ערוב must cover the whole city or each alley separately, never half the city.

steps.title: Next case begins: a city that was public and stays public
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא opens its next case: a city that was public from the start and is still public.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it was a public city, and it is still a public city,
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up the ברייתא's next case. The ruling for it comes in the following text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the ברייתא moves from a city that started private to one that was public from the start and is still public. This is a different case from the משנה's public-turned-private city in step 9, so do not assume the same rule applies. The ברייתא gives its ruling on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: It was a city of the many (a public city)

phrases.english: If it was a city of the many,

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיְתָה שֶׁל רַבִּים, וַהֲרֵי הִיא שֶׁל רַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The ברייתא moves from the private-turned-public case to a city that was always public
